title: Multiome Pre-processing for Zebrafish
text:
0.1 Who this is for
A practical, start-to-finish walkthrough of preprocessing 10X Chromium single-cell multiome data for zebrafish using the enhanced transcriptome annoations from the Lawson Lab.
You have multiome FASTQs from zebrafish, you want to run against a custom annotation (I.e., one or more custom genes included), and you need to get from raw reads to a joint object you can actually analyze.
Zebrafish (Danio rerio) is the worked example throughout, but the sticking points are general: building a reference from scratch, working around incomplete annotations, and leveraging both the gene expression and chromatin accessibility assays.
What you need before you start

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Motivation
This vignette will cover the basics of preprocessing 10X single-cell multiome data for zebrafish (Danio rerio) with Lawson Lab annotations. Currently, the 10X Epi Multiome kit supports rodent (mouse/rat), human, non-human primate, plant, insect, and marine organisms. However, processing requires additional steps when using a non-model organism, or an organism with custom genome annotations.
Zebrafish are a powerful model organism for single-cell studies as the embryos develop externally, rapidly, and in large clutches which allows for the collection of tightly staged timepoints as well as the dissociation of entire embryos rather than dissected tissues. While the organism itself contains a well-assembled reference genome, GRCz11, transcript annotation is uneven. Since the 10X Epi Multiome assay captures 3’ UTRs for gene expression, out-of-the-box gene annotation is tricky without a custom reference. The Lawson Lab annotation Lawson et al., 20201,2 extends 3’ UTRs and adds transcript models on top of GRCz11 to materially improve capture in 10X data.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1.1 What is multiome?
Multiome data refers to data which captures RNA transcript information (RNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility information (ATAC-seq) from the same single cell. These assays are primarily generated from 10X Genomics’ Chromium single cell multiome ATAC + Gene expression kits and BD Biosciences’ BD Rhapsody ATAC-Seq assay. These vignettes assume data were generated using 10X chemistry.
Sequencing one pool of cells for gene expression and a separate pool for ATAC helps improve cell type classification and resolution, but the two pools are independent and unmatched. Multiome assays get around this by profiling both modalities in the same single cell, allowing us to directly link regulatory states and gene expression. Gleaning information from both assays enables a more complete view of cellular states by linking what can happen (chromatin accessibility) with what is happening (gene expression). This linkage allows for more pointed questions that target causal and mechanistic insights into how the regulatory landscape influences gene expression to drive cellular state changes and dynamics.3


2.1.2 How does 10X Multiome Chemistry work?
A wide range of sample types can serve as input for the 10X Epi Multiome assay. Broadly, the workflow starts with isolated nuclei which are tagmented with the Tn5 transposase (ATAC) in bulk to preferentially cut nuclear DNA in regions of open chromatin. Transposed nuclei are partitioned into droplets (GEMs) with a single gel bead containing a unique 10X barcode. These unique barcodes are attached to available mRNA as well as transposed DNA fragments per single nucleus. Following incubation, GEMs are broken and pooled to facilitate amplification and library construction. Two aliquots are used: one for single-cell ATAC sequencing and one for single-cell GEX sequencing.4
For a detailed explanation of adapter/primer sequences and step-by-step library generation, see Teich Lab Single Cell Library Layouts 5

title: 3  Building a GRanges Reference Object
text:
3.1 Building a Reference Object
Downstream ATAC processing through Signac requires specific annotations in the form of a GRanges object carrying gene coordinates, IDs, and a gene_biotype column, which drives gene activity scoring and coverage plotting. The Lawson Lab annotations use in-house Lawson nomenclature, which is why 3 separate GTF files are required: one which carries the coordinates and features (shared with the features in your counts matrix), one which serves as a map between Lawson nomenclature and Ensembl nomenclature, and one native GRCz11 gtf which contains crucial biotype information. We use these 3 files together to collate all the necessary information per gene to build a master GRanges object.

title: 3  Building a GRanges Reference Object
text:
3.1.1 What you need


lawson_zebrafish.gtf: Contains the coordinates and features (i.e., the gene IDs appearing in the counts matrix).

V4.3.2.validated.gtf: Another Lawson Lab file containing both Lawson gene IDs and Ensembl transcript IDs in the same row. This file serves as a dictionary for mapping between Lawson nomenclature and Ensembl nomenclature.

Danio_rerio.GRCz11.113.gtf: This file carries gene biotype information, which will be required downstream for ATAC pre-processing functionality in Signac.







Warning



File 1 must be the same GTF that was passed to cellranger-arc mkref. If it is not, the gene IDs in the annotation object will not match the features in the counts matrix.



3.1.2 Software






Important



TODO: pin a reproducible environment. Options are a renv.lock committed alongside the book, a Conda environment YAML, or a container definition. Whichever is chosen, record the Bioconductor release as well as the package versions, since rtracklayer and GenomicRanges are versioned together.



library(rtracklayer)
library(GenomicRanges)


3.1.3 Setting paths

refDir <- "/users/mike/Desktop/multiome-tutorial/references/"

# Coordinates and features; the GTF used to build the CellRanger reference
lawsonGTFpath <- paste0(refDir, "GTFs/lawson_zebrafish.gtf")

# Dictionary: Lawson gene_id <-> Ensembl transcript_id
llV4path <- paste0(refDir, "GTFs/V4.3.2.validated.gtf")

# Reference annotation carrying gene_biotype
GRCz11path <- paste0(refDir, "GTFs/Danio_rerio.GRCz11.113.gtf")


3.1.4 Building the biotype dictionary
The chain runs in three steps. Ensembl supplies the biotype for each transcript ID. The validated Lawson GTF maps those transcript IDs to Lawson gene IDs. The result is a lookup table keyed on Lawson gene IDs.

# Ensembl: transcript_id -> gene_biotype
ens   <- rtracklayer::import(GRCz11path, format = "gtf")
ensTx <- as.data.frame(mcols(ens))
ensTx <- ensTx[ensTx$type == "transcript", c("transcript_id", "gene_biotype")]

# Lawson validated: gene_id <-> transcript_id
ll   <- rtracklayer::import(llV4path, format = "gtf")
llTx <- as.data.frame(mcols(ll))
llTx <- unique(llTx[llTx$type == "transcript", c("gene_id", "transcript_id")])

# Join and collapse to one biotype per Lawson gene_id
map <- merge(llTx, ensTx, by = "transcript_id", all.x = TRUE)
map <- map[!is.na(map$gene_biotype), c("gene_id", "gene_biotype")]
map <- map[!duplicated(map$gene_id), ]

The collapse on the last line is a decision rather than bookkeeping. A gene with several transcripts can map to more than one biotype. Taking the first asserts that any gene with a protein-coding transcript is a protein-coding gene. That is usually the intended behavior, but it is worth knowing how often it actually applies:

conflicts <- merge(llTx, ensTx, by = "transcript_id", all.x = TRUE)
conflicts <- conflicts[!is.na(conflicts$gene_biotype), ]
multi <- tapply(conflicts$gene_biotype, conflicts$gene_id,
                function(x) length(unique(x)))
table(multi)


3.1.5 Applying biotypes to the Lawson annotation

annotations <- rtracklayer::import(lawsonGTFpath)

idx <- match(mcols(annotations)$gene_id, map$gene_id)
mcols(annotations)$gene_biotype <- map$gene_biotype[idx]
mcols(annotations)$gene_biotype[is.na(mcols(annotations)$gene_biotype)] <- "Other"

Custom project-specific features (transgenes, reporters, knock-in constructs) have no Ensembl counterpart, so they fall through to "Other" and must be set explicitly. Match on gene_id, never on row position.

transgenes <- c("<transgene_1>", "<transgene_2>")

stopifnot(all(transgenes %in% mcols(annotations)$gene_id))

mcols(annotations)$gene_biotype[
  mcols(annotations)$gene_id %in% transgenes] <- "protein_coding"







Warning



Do not assign biotypes by row index. Row positions shift whenever the GTF is regenerated, a release is bumped, or a join expands and collapses the table. Indexing by position silently relabels arbitrary genes elsewhere in the genome, with no error to catch it. The stopifnot() above exists so that a renamed or missing transgene fails loudly instead.



3.1.6 Finalizing the object

keep <- c("type", "gene_id", "gene_name", "transcript_id", "gene_biotype")
mcols(annotations) <- mcols(annotations)[, keep]

genome(annotations) <- "GRCz11"

saveRDS(annotations,
        file = file.path(refDir, "Lawson_annotation_with_biotypes.Rds"))

Two details cause trouble later if skipped. Setting genome() matters because Annotation()<- and TSSEnrichment() warn or misbehave without it. And the sequence naming style has to match the fragments file:

seqlevelsStyle(annotations)
head(seqlevels(annotations))

Ensembl-derived annotations use 1, 2, 3; UCSC-derived files use chr1, chr2, chr3. A mismatch between the annotation and the fragments file produces zero overlaps rather than an error, which surfaces much later as an empty gene activity matrix or a TSS enrichment score of zero. Convert before saving if they differ:

seqlevelsStyle(annotations) <- "Ensembl"


3.1.7 Checks before moving on

table(mcols(annotations)$gene_biotype)
mcols(annotations)[mcols(annotations)$gene_id %in% transgenes, ]
length(unique(mcols(annotations)$gene_id))

Confirm that the biotype table is not overwhelmingly "Other", that the custom features are labeled as intended, and that the gene count falls in the expected range for the annotation. A large "Other" fraction usually means the dictionary join failed, most often because the two GTFs carry different identifier versions (ENSDART00000000001 against ENSDART00000000001.1). Strip the version suffix and rejoin if so.
